blocks.text: Drawing room in 3. Trenchard Manor, C. D., backed by interior, discovering table with luncheon spread. Large French window, R. 3 E., through which a fine English park is seen. Open archway, L. 3 E. Set balcony behind. Table, R., books and papers on it. Work basket containing wools and embroidery frame. A fashionable armchair and sofa, L. 2 E., small table near C. D. Stage handsomely set, costly furniture, carpet down, chairs, etc.
Very uncomfortable. I have no curtain to my bed.
And no wine at the second table.
And meaner servants I never seed.
I’m afraid Sir Edward is in a queer strait.

Mind your hown business instead hof your betters. I’m disgusted with you lower servants. When the wine merchant presents his bills, you men, hear me, say he’s been pressing for the last six months, do you?
Nor I, that the last year’s milliner’s bills have not been paid.
Nor I, that Miss Florence has not had no new dresses from London all winter.
And I can solemnly swear that his lordship’s hair has been faithfully bound in this bosom.
That’ll do, that’ll do; but to remember to check hidle curiosity is the first duty of men hin livery. Ha, ’ere hare the letters.
Why that be hin the United States of North Hamerica, and a main good place for poor folks.
But I know where Vermont be though.
Yes, shooting the wild helephants and buffalos what abound there.
Me fish for an ’at? Does she take me for an hangler?
And then go fish out my hat out of the pond, it’s not very deep.
This is a large letter with a large white envelope, red seal.
Now what will you give me for one?
Ah! Mon ami, you are to leave us. Good news, or bad?
Well, sometimes he brings a bag with a lock on it, sometimes newspapers, and sometimes letters, I suppothe.
I beg pardon, an event I am deeply interested in, that’s all. I beg pardon.
Why papa, it’s from dear brother Ned.
From my boy! Where is he? How is he? Read it.
Birds six feet high, what tremendous animals they must be.
Oh, I see what my brother means; a tribe of indians called Crows, not birds.
Oh, I thought you meant those creatures with wigs on them.
Birds with wings, that’s the idea.
An American branch of the family.
An Apollo of the prairie; yes, with a strong nasal twang, and a decided taste for tobacco and cobblers.
Florence, you forget that he is a Trenchard, and no true Trenchard would have a liking for cobblers or low people of that kind.
I hate him, whatever he is, coming here to rob poor cousin Mary of her grandmother’s guineas.
Florence, how often must I request you not to speak of Mary Meredith as your cousin?
Oh, yeth, I know what syllabubs is﻿—yeth﻿—yeth.
Why, I don’t believe you do know what they are.
No, it’s not a bit like the idea. What you mean are called cherubims.
What, those things that look like oranges, with wings on them?
Not a bit like it. Well, after luncheon you must go with me and I’ll introduce you to my cousin Mary and syllabubs.
I never can forget﻿—when I can recollect.
Then recollect that you have an appointment with me after luncheon.
Well, what have you after luncheon?
Well, sometimes I have a glass of brandy with an egg in it, sometimes a run ’round the duck-pond, sometimes a game of checkers﻿—that’s for exercise, and perhaps a game of billiards.
No, no; you have with me after luncheon, an ap﻿—an ap﻿—
She is a great sufferer, my dear.
What sort of a night had she?
Oh, a very refreshing one, thanks to the draught you were kind enough to prescribe for her, Lord Dundreary.
What! Has Lord Dundreary been prescribing for Georgina?
Yeth. You see I gave her a draught that cured the effect of the draught, and that draught was a draft that didn’t pay the doctor’s bill. Didn’t that draught﻿—
Good gracious! what a number of draughts. You have almost a game of draughts.
That wath a joke, that wath.
She don’t see it. Don’t you see﻿—a game of drafts﻿—pieces of wound wood on square pieces of leather. That’s the idea. Now, I want to put your brains to the test. I want to ask you a whime.
A whime is a widdle, you know.
Yeth; one of those things, like﻿—why is so-and-so or somebody like somebody else.
Oh, I see, you mean a conundrum.
Why, what in earth has a dog’s tail to do with a cart?
When it moves about, you know. A horse makes a cart move, so does a dog make his tail move.
Wags the letter in her hand.
Well, a wagon and a cart are the same thing, ain’t they! That’s the idea﻿—it’s the same thing.
They are not the same. In the case of your conundrum there’s a very great difference.
Now I’ve got another. Why does a dog waggle his tail?
Upon my word, I never inquired.
Because the tail can’t waggle the dog. Ha! Ha!
Ha! ha! Is that your own, Dundreary?
Now I’ve got one, and this one is original.
No, no, don’t spoil the last one.
Yeth; but this is extremely interesting.
Do you think so, Lord Dundreary?

Yeth. Miss Georgina likes me to tell her my jokes. By the by, talking of that lonely sufferer, isn’t she an interesting invalid? They do say that’s what’s the matter with me. I’m an interesting invalid.
Oh, that accounts for what I have heard so many young ladies say﻿—Florence, dear, don’t you think Lord Dundreary’s extremely interesting? I never knew what they meant before.
Yeth, the doctor recommends me to drink donkey’s milk.
An eye for color! Yes, especially green.
Why, that wath a joke, that wath.
Florence, dear, I must leave you to represent me to my guests. These letters will give me a great deal of business today.
Well, papa, remember I am your little clerk and person of all work.
Dear papa, how I wish you would get another agent.
Nonsense, Florence, impossible. He knows my affairs. His father was agent for the late Baronet. He’s one of the family, almost.
Papa, I have implicit faith in my own judgement of faces. Depend upon it, that man is not to be trusted.
Remember the archery meeting, papa. It is at three.
Miss Florence, will you be kind enough to tell Miss Georgina all about that American relative of yours.
Yes, that’s about the average height.
If you please, Miss, ’ere’s a gent what says he’s hexpected.
What’s his name? Where’s his card?

He didn’t tell me his name, Miss, and when I haxed him for his card ’e said ’e had a whole pack in his valise, and if I ’ad a mine ’e’d play me a game of seven hup. He says he has come to stay, and he certainly looks as if he didn’t mean to go.
Do you mean Sir Edward Trenchard, sir?
He is not present, but I am his daughter.
Well, I guess that’ll fit about as well if you tell this darned old shoat to take me to my room.
What does he mean by shoat?
He calls me a ’oss, Miss, I suppose I shall be a hox next, or perhaps an ’ogg.
Wal, darn me if you ain’t the consarnedest old shoat I ever did see since I was baptized Asa Trenchard.
Ah! then it is our American cousin. Glad to see you﻿—my brother told us to expect you.

Wal, yes, I guess you do b’long to my family. I’m Asa Trenchard, born in Vermont, suckled on the banks of Muddy Creek, about the tallest gunner, the slickest dancer, and generally the loudest critter in the state. You’re my cousin, be you? Wal, I ain’t got no objections to kiss you, as one cousin ought to kiss another.
Gives letter and attempts to kiss her.
Gives her hand, which he shakes heartily.
Yeth, Miss Florence. The room and I have got through with each other, yeth.
Concentrated essence of baboons, what on earth is that?
He’s mad. Yes, Miss Florence, I’ve done with that room. The rooks crowed so that they racked my brain.
You don’t mean to say that you’ve got any brains.
Old Mark Trenchard died very rich, did he not, Florence?
He’s not at all romantic, is he, mamma?
But what are we to do with him?
It’s so seldom I get an idea that when I do get one it startles me. Let us get a pickle bottle.
Yeth; one of those things with glass sides.
Oh! you mean a glass case.
Now he thinks he’s a horse. I’ve heard of a great jackass, and I dreampt of a jackass, but I don’t believe there is any such insect.
Well, cousin, I hope you made yourself comfortable.
Well, no, I can’t say as I did. You see there was so many all-fired fixins in my room I couldn’t find anything I wanted.
What was it you couldn’t find in your room?

Yes, soft soap. I reckon you know what that is. However, I struck a pump in the kitchen, slicked my hair down a little, gave my boots a lick of grease, and now I feel quite handsome; but I’m everlastingly dry.
You’ll find ale, wine and luncheon on the side table.

Wal, I don’t know as I’ve got any appetite. You see comin’ along on the cars I worried down half a dozen ham sandwiches, eight or ten boiled eggs, two or three pumpkin pies and a string of cold sausages﻿—and﻿—Wal, I guess I can hold on till dinnertime.
Did that illustrious exile eat all that? I wonder where he put it?
I’m as dry as a sap-tree in August.
Why, does he want Mary to slap Jack?
Pork’s been here, but he’s left.
And where on airth’s the clam chowder?
What do you mean by fixins?
Why, brandy, rum, gin and whiskey. We’ll make them all useful.
Oh! I thought he meant the gas fixins.
Oh, don’t mind him! That’s only an American joke.
A joke! Do you call that a joke? To make a sick girl squirm like a mud bank on an eel’s skin?

Yes, I’ll give you a drink that’ll make your whiskers return under your chin, which is their natural location. Now, ladies and gentlemen, what’ll you have, Whiskey Skin, Brandy Smash, Sherry Cobbler, Mint Julep or Jersey Lightning?
Oh, I want a Mint Julep.
Library in Trenchard Manor. Oriel Window, L. C., with curtains. Two chairs and table brought on at change.
And now to show this pompous baronet the precipice on which he stands.
Enter Murcott, with green bag and papers.
I’ll do my best, sir. But, oh! do tell them to keep liquor out of my way. I can’t keep from it now, try as I will, and I try hard enough, God help me!
Confound it, why harass me with details, these infernal particulars? Have you made out the total?
Four thousand, eight hundred and thirty pounds, nine shillings and sixpence.
Well, of course we must find means of settling this extortion.
I, as your agent, must stoop to detail, you must allow me to repeat, if possible.
Why, you don’t say there will be any difficulty in raising the money?
What means would you suggest, Sir Edward.
Curse your impudence, pay them off.
Confound it, sir, which of us is the agent? Am I to find you brains for your own business?
No, Sir Edward, I can furnish the brains, but what I ask of you is to furnish the money.
There must be money somewhere, I came into possession of one of the finest properties in Hampshire only twenty-six years ago, and now you mean to tell me I cannot raise 4,000 pounds?
The fact is distressing, Sir Edward, but so it is.
There, Sir Edward, you are under a mistake. The Ravensdale property is deeply encumbered, to nearly its full value.
I have found among my father’s papers a mortgage of that very property to him.
To your father! My father’s agent?
Yes, bearing date the year after the great contested election for the county, on which the late Sir Edward patriotically spent sixty thousand pounds for the honor of not being returned to Parliament.
Sir, do you know that if this be true I am something like a beggar, and your father something like a thief.
I see the first plainly, Sir Edward, but not the second.
Do you forget sir, that your father was a charity boy, fed, clothed by my father?
And do you mean to tell me, sir, that your father repaid that kindness by robbing his benefactor?
Certainly not, but by advancing money to that benefactor when he wanted it, and by taking the security of one of his benefactor’s estates, as any prudent man would under the circumstances.
Why, then, sir, the benefactor’s property is yours.
Pardon me, the legal estate you have your equity of redemption. You have only to pay the money and the estate is yours as before.
How dare you, sir, when you have just shown me that I cannot raise five hundred pounds in the world. Oh! Florence, why did I not listen to you when you warned me against this man?
By marrying your daughter to the mortgagee.
I never take an angry man at his word, Sir Edward. Give a few moments reflection to my offer, you can have me kicked out afterwards.
Nothing, the dizziness I’ve had lately.
Brandy in the evening, brandy in the morning, brandy all night. What a fool you are, Murcott.
Who knows that as well as I do?
If you would but keep the money out of your mouth, there’s the making of a man in you yet.

You owe Sir Edward revenge, do you not? You shall have a rare revenge on him, that mortgage you found last week puts the remainder of the property in my reach, and I close my hand on it unless he will consent to my terms.
You can drive a hard bargain. I know.
And a rare price I ask for his forbearance, Abel﻿—his daughter’s hand.
Chamber in 3. at Trenchard Manor. Large shower bath near R. 3 E. Toilet table with draw, L. 2 E. Small bottle in draw with red sealing wax on cork.
Will you have the kindness to give me your keys, hif you please, sir?
What do you want with my keys?
To put your things away in the wardrobe, sir.

Wal, I calculate if my two shirts, three bosoms, four collars, and two pair of socks were to get into that everlasting big bunk, they’d think themselves so all-fired small I should never be able to crawl into them again.
Will you take a baath before you dress?
I suppose you mean a bath. Wal, man, I calkalate I ain’t going to expose myself to the shakes by getting into cold water in this cruel cold climate of yours, so make tracks.
Assistance! what to get out of my unmentionables and into them again? Wal, ’spose I do, what then?
Just ring the bell, hi’ll hattend you.
Red sealing wax on the top?
Orrable, what an hawful situation, to be sure.
Miss Florence begged me to say she had borrowed a costume for you, for the harchery meeting, sir.
What do you mean by the harchery meeting?
Where they shoot with bows and harrows.

There goes another of them, oh! you need’nt look for them, you can’t find ’em when you want ’em. Now you just take my compliments to Miss Trenchard when I goes out shooting with injurious weapons I always wears my own genuine shooting costume. That’s the natural buff tipped off with a little red paint.
Slips partly inside shower bath, pulls rope, water comes down.

No, my dear Augusta, you must be very careful. I don’t by any means want you to give up De Boots, his expectations are excellent, but, pray be attentive to this American savage, as I rather think he will prove the better match of the two, if what I hear of Mark Trenchard’s property be correct.
And look more cheerful, my love.
I am so tired, ma, of admiring things I hate.
Yes, my poor love, yet we must all make sacrifices to society. Look at your poor sister, with the appetite.
What am I to be enthusiastic about with that American, Ma?
Here he comes, ma. What a ridiculous figure he looks in that dress, ha! ha!
Yes, one of those dresses in which you hunt the buffalo.
The first buffalo I see about here I shall hunt up for you.
Oh, you Americans are so clever, and so acute.
Yes, we’re ’cute, we are; know soft solder when we see it.
Yes, I’ll be there like a thousand of brick.
Spoiled what, my lord; why, a most magnificent sneeze!
I am very sorry, my lord.
Now that I can speak alone with you, tell me about that hair dye. Have you found it?
Not a trace of it, my lord.
If you don’t find it, I’ll discharge you.
Will you try and strengthen your limbs with a gentle walk in the garden?
Yes, Miss Georgina; but they’re very strengthening flowers, you know.
Yes, my lord, you are always right.
Do you know I’m getting to be very robust?
Would I could share that fault with you; but I am so delicate.
If you were robust I should not love you as I do. It would deprive you of that charm which enchains me to your lovely side, which﻿—which﻿—
Oh, my lord, my lord! I’m going to faint.
And I’m going to sneeze, you faint while I sneeze.
Do you know what a sneeze is?
She never sneezed. I’ll tell you what a sneeze is. Imagine a very large spider.

No, no, I don’t mean a real spider, only an imaginary one, a large spider getting up your nose, and all of a sudden, much to his disgust, he discovers he has put his foot in it and can’t get it out again.
For the spider, yes, and not very pleasant for the nose.
Oh! my lord, do take me to mamma.
No, you lovely sufferer, let’s walk a little more.
No, my lord, I’m too delicate.
How would you like the left wing of a canary bird?
No, my lord, it’s too strong for me.
Oh! for one minute’s clear head, Miss Florence.
I presume you are the writer of this?
You address me as an old acquaintance, but I do not recognize you.
So much the better. So much the better.
I hate mystery, sir; but you see I have come to rendezvous. I must know to whom I am speaking.
As frank as ever. I am Abel Murcott.

Do not be ashamed, I have not the strength to injure you, if I had the evil. In this shabby, broken down drunkard you need not fear the madman, who years ago forgot in his frantic passion the gulf that lay between your station and his own. I am harmless except to myself.
Speak on, sir; I hear you.
I come to tell you of your father’s ruin, his utter ruin.
Then beggary stares him in the face. Poor father, what a sad blow for him. Is that all, sir?
On consideration of settling on you the Ravensdale Estate.
And my father, how did he listen to such insolence?

You know as well as I do how he would hear such a proposal, at first a torrent of rage, then the strong ebb of selfishness set in, and he consented to listen to the terms, to view them as something to be considered, to consider them.
Good Heavens, can this be true? No, I will not believe it of my father, and from such lips.
I am past taking offence or feeling scorn, I have carried more than can be heaped upon me, but I did not come only to give you warning of your danger.

Wal, it wasn’t purpose, I went in there to take a snooze, I heard you talking and I thought it wouldn’t be polite of me not to listen to what you had to say. I’m a rough sort of a customer, and don’t know much about the ways of great folks. But I’ve got a cool head, a stout arm, and a willing heart, and I think I can help you, just as one cousin ought to help another.
Well, I do think you are honest.
Yes, we will trust him, go on.
Have ye, now? Well, if a Yankee lawyer had done such a thing he would have Judge Lynch after him in no time.
You can but find that release, we may unmask this diabolical fiend and save you.
No, no, no, if you did but know the hope of seeing you has roused all the manhood that drink and misery has left me. God bless you, Miss Florence.

Park in 4. Rural cottage, L. 1 E., adjoining which, and projecting on stage an inside view of a dairy with sloping roof, painting backing to look like milk pans. The whole scene should have a picturesque appearance. Garden fence run across back, ornamental gate or archway, R. 3 E. Pigeon house on pole near dairy, L. C. Spinning wheel inside cottage door, one or two rustic benches, R. and L.
Oh, Wickens, you are there. How kind of you to help me with the milk pails today, when all the lads and lasses have given themselves a holiday to see the shooting.
Ah, Miss Mary, you ought to be among then, with a green hat and feather, if all had their rights.
Now, Miss Mary, what can I do for you?
Let me see; well, really, I do believe, Wickens, I’ve nothing to do but amuse myself.
Dang it, Miss, that’s a pity, cos I can’t help you at that, you see.
I congratulate you, sir, and am happy to see you.
That will do for a beginning.
Why have you left the archery, Florence?
You? Grave business? Why I thought you never had any graver business than being very pretty, very amiable, and very ready to be amused.
You are very polite. This is my domain, sir, and I shall be happy to show you, that is, if you understand anything about a dairy.
Yes, by the way, do you understand anything about dairies in America?
Yes, sir, I milk the cows, set up the milk, superintend the churning and make the cheese.
Wal, darn me if you ain’t the first raal right down useful gal I’ve seen on this side the pond.
What’s that, sir? Do you want to make me jealous?
Oh, no, you needn’t get your back up, you are the right sort too, but you must own you’re small potatoes, and few in a hill compared to a gal like that.
Will you be kind enough to translate that for me, for I don’t understand American yet.
Ah, it’s very clear now; but, cousin, do tell me what you mean by calling me small potatoes.
Wal, you can sing and paint, and play on the pianner, and in your own particular circle you are some pumpkins.
Some pumpkins, first I am small potatoes, and now I’m some pumpkins.
But she, she can milk cows, set up the butter, make cheese, and, darn me, if them ain’t what I call raal downright feminine accomplishments.
I do believe you are right cousin, so Mary do allow me to congratulate you upon not being small potatoes.
Well, cousin, what do you think of her?
Don’t show it to me, I don’t want to look at it, the fortune should have come to Mary, she is the only relation in the direct line.
Say, cousin, you’ve not told her that darned property was left to me, have you?
Do you think I had the heart to tell her of her misfortune?
Say, cousin, I guess I’ve got you on a string now, as I heard you say this morning.
Wal, what if you have, didn’t I see you casting sheep’s eyes at that sailor man this morning? Ah, I reckon I’ve got you on a string now. Say, has he got that ship yet?
No, he hasn’t, though I’ve used all my powers of persuasion with that Lord Dundreary, and his father has so much influence with the admiralty.
Wal, din’t he drop like a smoked possum?
There you go, more American. No, he said he was very sorry, but he couldn’t.
I shall be missed at the archery grounds. Will you take me back?
Offers arm and takes her to dairy.
Takes her round stage back to dairy.
Well, but where are you going now?
I was just going round. I say, cousin, don’t you think you could find your way back alone.
Thank you, my lord; you are so kind to me, and I am so delicate.
Yes, you look delicate, dear; how is she this morning, any better?
When she recovers, she’ll be better.
I’m afraid you don’t take good care of her, you are so rough.
Now, let me administer to your wants. How would you like a roast chestnut?
No, my lord, I’m too delicate.
Well, then, a peanut; there is a great deal of nourishment in peanuts.
Then what can I do for you?
If you please, ask the dairy maid to let me have a seat in the dairy. I am afraid of the draft, here.
No, my lord, that’s the pigeon house.
What do they keep in pigeon houses? Oh! pigeons, to be sure; they couldn’t keep donkeys up there, could they? That’s the dairy, I suppothe?
What do they keep in dairies?
What’s the name of that animal with a head on it? No, I don’t mean that, all animals have heads. I mean those animals with something growing out of their heads.
A cow growing out of his head?
A cow! well, that accounts for the milk and butter; but I don’t see the eggs; cows don’t give eggs; then there’s the cheese﻿—do you like cheese?
I have no brother. I’m so delicate.
She’s so delicate, she hasn’t got a brother. Well, if you had a brother do you think he’d like cheese?
I don’t know; do please take me to the dairy.

I beg you pardon, Miss Georgina, but I find upon enquiry that cows don’t give sardines. But I’ve arranged it with the dairy maid so that you can have a seat by the window that overlooks the cow house and the pig sty, and all the pretty things.
They go up to cottage door.
Comes down, takes off hat, looking in it.
Lowers one, then the other, they trip him up.
Goes hopping upstage, stumbling over against spinning wheel. Looks at yarn on stick.
That is a steam engine, and will bust in about a minute.
Say, whiskers, I want to ask a favor of you.
Spoiled what! why a magnificent sneeze.
Oh! was that what you was trying to get through you?
Wal, what do you think of him, on an average?
Think of a man on an average?
Wal, I think he’s a real hoss, and he wants a ship.
Well if he’s a real hoss, he must want a carriage.
Darn me, if that ain’t good.
What, are you at that again?
He says I’ve got a wart. I’ve got the influenza.
That’s it exactly. I want your influence, sir, to get that ship.
Yes, darn me, if that ain’t good.
For you. Ha! ha! One on that Yankee.
Well done, Britisher. Wal, now, about that ship?
He’s hard of hearing, and thinks he’s in a balloon. Mister.
He thinks he can hear with his nose. I say﻿—
Now he thinks he’s a musical instrument. I say﻿—
You stutter. I’ll give you a k﻿—k﻿—k﻿—
No you won’t give me a kick.
I’ll give you a c﻿—c﻿—card to a doctor and he’ll c﻿—c﻿—c﻿—
No he won’t kick me, either.
He’s idiotic. I don’t mean that, he’ll cure you.
Wal, if you’re cured I want to stay sick. He must be a mighty smart man.
A very clever man, he is.
Wal, darn me, if there ain’t a physiological change taking place. Your whiskers at this moment﻿—
Yes, about the ends they’re as black as a niggers in billing time, and near the roots they’re all speckled and streaked.
My hair dye. My dear sir.
He’s mad, he’s deaf, he squints, stammers and he’s a hopper.
Now, look here, you get the Lieutenant a ship and I’ll give you the bottle. It’s a fine swap.
What the devil is a swap?
Well, you give me the ship, and I’ll give you the bottle to boot.
What do I want of your boots? I haven’t got a ship about me.
You’d better make haste or your whiskers will be changed again. They’ll be a pea green in about a minute.
Now to distribute the prizes, and drink to the health of the winner of the golden arrow.
And there must stand the hero of the day. Come, kneel down.
I am going to crown you Captain of the Archers of Trenchard Manor.
Takes glasses, Starts on seeing men in livery.
Dairy set as before in Act 2nd, Scene 2.
Miss Mary, I wish you’d leave off those everlasting dairy fixings, and come and take a hand of chat along with me.
What, and leave my work? Why, when you first came here, you thought I could not be too industrious.

Well, I think so yet, Miss Mary, but I’ve got a heap to say to you, and I never can talk while you’re moving about so spry among them pans, pails and cheeses. First you raise one hand and then the other, and well, it takes the gumption right out of me.
Well, no, Miss Mary, that won’t do, neither; them eyes of yourn takes my breath away.
Well, I don’t know, Miss Mary, but, darn me, if you could do anything that wasn’t so tarnal neat and handsome, that a fellow would want to keep on doing nothing else all the time.
Oh, if you only knew how it helps me to keep my eyes off you, Miss Mary.
But you needn’t keep your eyes off me.

I’m afraid I must, my eyes are awful tale-tellers, and they might be saying something you wouldn’t like to hear, and that might make you mad, and then you’d shut up school, and send me home feeling about as small as a tadpole with his tail bobbed off.
Don’t be alarmed, I don’t think I will listen to any tales that your eyes may tell unless they’re tales I like and ought to hear.
If I thought they’d tell any other, Miss Mary, I pluck them right out and throw them in the first turnip patch I came to.
And now tell me more about your home in America. Do you know I’ve listened to your stories until I’m half a backwoodsman’s wife already?
Yes, I can shut my eyes and almost fancy I see your home in the backwoods. There are your two sisters running about in their sunbonnets.
Then I can see the smoke curling from the chimney, then men and boys working in the fields.
The girls milking the cows, and everybody so busy.
And then at night, home come your four big brothers from the hunt laden with game, tired and footsore, and covered with snow.
Then how we lasses bustle about to prepare supper. The fire blazes on the hearth, while your good old mother cooks the slapjacks.
